newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Greece to legalise throngs of Albanian workers.
newsitem.headline: Greece to legalise throngs of Albanian workers.

text.p: Greece agreed on Tuesday to legalise the status of hundreds of thousands of illegal Albanian immigrants in exchange for help in fighting cross-border crime imported from the troubled Balkan state.

In a protocol, signed by visiting Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos and his Albanian counterpart Paskal Milo, the two countries agreed to issue temporary work permits to Albanians, who are now often summarily expelled from Greece.
"Mr Pangalos promised that Albanian immigrants in Greece will be treated equally with other immigrants. This is the best news for Albania," Albanian Foreign Minister Paskal Milo told reporters.
But an offer to lend Albania $20 million has stumbled on objections from Tirana to the conditions of the loan and may not materialise, Greek diplomats in Tirana told Reuters.

Greece, eager to see stability restored to Albania, has sent a team of ministers to help reorganise its shattered economy, army and police, in the first foreign visit to Tirana since a new Albanian government was elected in June.

Relations between the neighbouring countries plummeted in 1994, when Greece expelled thousands of Albanian immigrants in response to the trial of Albanian ethnic Greek leaders for spying. Ties were patched up again a year later.

A heavy inflow of illegal Albanian immigrants fleeing violence and poverty, now estimated at about 300,000, has taxed the Greek economy and police forces have been facing a new wave of crime across Greece's northern border.
"We have agreed with Albanian authorities to make a joint effort to hold back the wave of immigrants," Deputy Labour Minister Christos Protopapas told reporters.

More than 1,500 people have been killed in Albania since March, when bogus pyramid investment schemes collapsed and left tens of thousands destitute. Survival for many Albanian families hinges on workers' remittances from abroad.

Albanians looted an estimated one million weapons from army and police depots, triggering months of anarchy which led to the fall of the Democratic Party government and the resignation of president Sali Berisha.

Greece, keen to back the government of Socialist Prime Minister Fatos Nano, has also brought deputy ministers of the economy, defence and public works to Albania to help restore order and boost development.
"There will be continuous cooperation on all these issues," Pangalos told reporters.
Greek Public Order Minister George Romeos, whose ministry has borne the brunt of the new crime wave, secured the help of Albanian authorities in better patrolling of borders.
"We also agreed to train their police and continue to supply them with equipment," the diplomat said.

Romeos has complained that crime committed by Albanian nationals in Greece had risen considerably since March. Southern Albania remains at the mercy of armed bands, and roads linking towns to the capital are often violent.

The world community has been eager to help Albania stabilise after months of anarchy. International donors are due to meet in Brussels in October to examine ways to provide aid in the form of approved projects.
